Introduction

Accurate prediction of daily high temperatures is a critical component of modern weather forecasting, influencing decision-making across sectors such as energy management, transportation, and public safety. Reliable temperature forecasts support efficient resource allocation, including electricity demand planning and climate-sensitive operations in aviation and infrastructure. In recent years, advances in data-driven modeling have complemented traditional numerical weather prediction methods, offering improved accuracy and adaptability for localized forecasting tasks. Machine learning techniques, particularly ensemble methods, have demonstrated strong performance in capturing nonlinear relationships within meteorological data. Among these, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) has emerged as a powerful and efficient algorithm for predictive modeling in structured datasets (Chen and Guestrin 2016).

Recent research has increasingly explored the use of machine learning techniques to enhance weather prediction accuracy, particularly in short-term forecasting applications. Ensemble learning methods such as XGBoost have been shown to outperform traditional statistical models and complement numerical weather prediction systems by effectively capturing nonlinear relationships and correcting systematic biases (Dong et al. 2023). Prior studies have applied XGBoost to tasks such as precipitation forecasting and bias correction of meteorological outputs, demonstrating improved predictive performance across diverse geographic regions (Dong et al. 2023). Additionally, comparative analyses of machine learning algorithms highlight the robustness and computational efficiency of gradient boosting approaches when applied to structured environmental data (Zhou 2023), (Singh and Rawat 2023). Despite these advances, many studies focus on regional or large-scale forecasting problems, leaving opportunities for more localized, site-specific modeling of daily temperature using high-frequency observational data. XGBoost has also been documented in tutorial and use-case contexts for its implementation and interpretability in applied machine learning problems (Wiens et al. 2025).

This study focuses on predicting daily high temperatures at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) using high-frequency observational data obtained from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) (Environmental Information (NCEI) 2026). The dataset consists of five-minute interval weather measurements, providing a detailed temporal view of atmospheric conditions that can be aggregated to support daily forecasting tasks. By leveraging this granular data, the study aims to capture short-term variability and improve the accuracy of daily maximum temperature predictions. An XGBoost regression model is developed to model the relationship between meteorological features and daily high temperature, with an emphasis on evaluating its predictive performance in a localized airport environment. This approach provides a practical framework for applying machine learning techniques to site-specific temperature forecasting using publicly available observational data.

The primary objective of this study is to develop and evaluate an XGBoost-based model for predicting daily high temperatures at LAX using aggregated ASOS observational data. Model performance is assessed using a comprehensive set of regression evaluation metrics, including MAE, MSE, RMSE, \(R^2\), MAPE, and explained variance, to provide a thorough assessment of prediction accuracy, error magnitude, and model fit. In addition, the study examines feature importance to better understand the contribution of key meteorological variables to model predictions. By focusing on a single, well-instrumented location and leveraging high-resolution data, this research aims to demonstrate the applicability of machine learning methods for localized temperature forecasting. The findings contribute to the growing body of work on data-driven weather prediction and highlight the potential of XGBoost as a practical tool for operational forecasting tasks, consistent with prior statistical temperature prediction work in California and broader North America (Dias et al. 2018).

Methods

  • Detail the models or algorithms used.

  • Justify your choices based on the problem and data.

The common non-parametric regression model is \(Y_i = m(X_i) + \varepsilon_i\), where \(Y_i\) can be defined as the sum of the regression function value \(m(x)\) for \(X_i\). Here \(m(x)\) is unknown and \(\varepsilon_i\) some errors. With the help of this definition, we can create the estimation for local averaging i.e. \(m(x)\) can be estimated with the product of \(Y_i\) average and \(X_i\) is near to \(x\). In other words, this means that we are discovering the line through the data points with the help of surrounding data points. The estimation formula is printed below (R Core Team 2019):

\[ M_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} W_n (X_i) Y_i \tag{1} \]\(W_n(x)\) is the sum of weights that belongs to all real numbers. Weights are positive numbers and small if \(X_i\) is far from \(x\).

Another equation:

\[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 +\varepsilon_i \]
